title: Throttle
description: Throttle caps invocations to one per `ms` window — extra calls during the cool-down are dropped (leading-edge variant). Built with an injectable clock so tests advance time deterministically.

notes: Leading-edge throttle fires on the first call of each window; trailing-edge would defer to the window end. Both are valid — pick one and document it.
Initialize `lastFired = -Infinity` (or any sentinel < -ms) so the very first call always fires.
Dropped calls are lost — no queueing. Debounce keeps the latest args; throttle does not.

questions.q: Three calls within one ms window to a leading-edge throttled fn invoke the underlying fn how many times?
What is the key difference between debounce and throttle?
options: Throttle uses promises; debounce does not
Debounce delays until quiet; throttle caps the rate (at most one per window)
Throttle queues calls; debounce drops them
To make `_now - lastFired >= ms` true on the very first call
JavaScript requires sentinel values for numbers
It hides the variable from the closure

questions.q: If the underlying fn is called inside the cool-down window, what happens to its args?
options: Queued and applied at window end
Dropped — leading-edge throttle does not buffer

exercises.prompt: Complete the throttle: fire on the first call, drop calls within ms, fire again once the window passes.

blanks.hint: advance the fake clock by delta

L3.prompt: Implement throttle(fn, ms) leading-edge with injectable clock. Show: first call fires, two more within window drop, advance past window, next call fires.
L3.expectedOutput:
calls=1 last=a
calls=1 last=a
calls=2 last=d
hints: Track only `lastFired` — no pending args, no scheduled callback.
On each call, compare _now - lastFired against ms; fire and update lastFired only if the gap is large enough.
tick(delta) is the only way time moves — there's no real setTimeout.
